doc.title: Bob Stewart interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Adjusting as ensemble tuba, and tuba technical questions
summary: He adapted tuba parts to the bass player, added unwritten touches; they discuss tuba range and fourth trombone parts at LaGuardia.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Right. Did you get the sense, when you were playing ensemble tuba, did the bass player in that group need to do any adjusting in their note choices?

I did the adjusting because in a lot of bands, with the exception of like Carla Bley or Gil Evans, they didn’t really know how to write. Early arrangements of Frank Foster with tuba in it, he wasn’t writing well. He wasn’t writing great tuba parts. So quite often my part was either big half note versions of the bass part or half notes paralleling the baritone saxophone. Later on he started writing differently for the tuba. I’m not sure whether I influenced that or he just started hearing it a little better, or he started understanding how to write for it and what to do, how it could fit into the ensemble better. But what I would do during the period where he was just writing me half notes, I started doing things like instead of going [scats] I’d say [scats]. I would put little chromatic things leading into the note and quite often I’d hear the bass player doing that so I would do it with him. And the

bass would look over to me and smile. So I got certain — I would take certain liberties with the music and the band leaders would never say anything. They’d say, “Oh that’s cool, yeah okay,” they’d just nod their head. So it allowed me to play what wasn’t on the paper and get the okay from the band leader and from the bass player. So I learned how to add things, little things to the big band that weren’t on the paper that helped push where the accents of things were.
Probably learning that trad music in the beginning helped develop your hearing.

Oh sure. For sure. Understanding exactly where that rhythm section thing was, rather than, I wasn’t just an ensemble horn that didn’t know the possibility was there. I was an ensemble horn that had played bass lines and things in two-beat songs.
Just a technical thing — does the tuba sound an octave lower?
No it sounds where you write it.
It sounds where you write it.
It sounds exactly where you write it.
Because sometimes you see, you know a high school band or something that’s short of a trombone and you’ll see a tuba on the fourth trombone stand.

Quite often I tried to do, when I was teaching high school at LaGuardia High School, the performing arts high school in New York, I would — we had a couple of great tuba players that came through that school and I would put them on that fourth part. And quite often the fourth part would go up high from time to time and these cats learned how to blend with the other three trombones so that they didn’t miss a beat. There were some monster players.
